query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal‐element alloys (MPEAs) exposed to harsh high‐temperature oxidizing environments, the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized surface layer promotes oxidation resistance and material integrity by serving as a diffusion barrier that retards oxygen ingress and supports self-healing oxide formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained multiprincipal-element alloy (e.g., similar in composition to CoCrFeMnNi) without pre-induced nanocrystallinity.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing (e.g., controlled deformation or rapid thermal cycling) designed to induce dynamic amorphization and generate an ultra‐nanocrystalline near‐surface layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidizing environment (e.g., 600–900 °C in air) maintained for sustained periods to evaluate oxidation kinetics and mechanical property retention.
generation.structural_mediator: The ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer characterized by high-angle grain boundaries produced via dynamic amorphization.
generation.mechanism: The high density of grain boundaries in the amorphized nanolayer acts as an effective barrier against oxygen diffusion and encourages the formation of a mixed metal-oxide scale that is self-healing, thereby preserving the material's bulk mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained alloy, the processed alloy with the nanocrystalline layer will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation rates, lower oxide scale spallation, and better retention of mechanical properties (e.g., reduced brittleness or creep under thermal cycling).
generation.baseline: The coarse-grained multiprincipal-element alloy with no induced dynamic amorphization (no pre-existing nanocrystalline surface structure) subjected to the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for MPEAs with similar compositional complexity and microstructural evolution in the temperature range of approximately 600–900 °C in oxidizing environments. It might not apply to alloys that cannot undergo dynamic amorphization or possess significantly different phase structures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the nanocrystalline surface on oxidation kinetics and long-term mechanical performance is not yet established, and the extent to which self-healing oxide formation contributes independently requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical MPEA samples: one set undergoes thermomechanical treatment to induce dynamic amorphization (ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer) and the other remains untreated (coarse-grained). Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions (600–900 °C in air) for an extended period. Compare the oxidation kinetics, oxide scale integrity, and mechanical properties (e.g., wear resistance, microhardness) post-exposure.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (using SEM/EDS)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via XRD)
Mechanical property retention (through nanoindentation or tensile testing)
Grain size and morphology at the surface (via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar oxide scale growth, spallation, and degradation in mechanical properties) compared to the untreated coarse-grained samples, then the hypothesis that the dynamic amorphized ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer governs improved oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
